places.name: Arthurs Seat
places.factualLede: Arthurs Seat is the highest point on the Mornington Peninsula, rising above Dromana with views across Port Phillip Bay and the surrounding hinterland.
places.intro: Arthurs Seat is the Peninsula's high point — the ridge-top lookout, gondola, gardens and hairpin road that orient the whole region in one view. It is less a village than a landmark, but for visitors it behaves like a destination: come up for the bay panorama, the Eagle, short summit walks and the first real sense of how the beaches, vineyards and villages fit together.
tldr: Arthurs Seat is the Peninsula's highest point and one of its clearest orientation stops.
Best for: first-time visitors, families, view-seekers and anyone trying to understand the Peninsula's geography quickly.
Signature experience: the Arthurs Seat Eagle gondola and summit lookout on a clear morning.
Pair it with Dromana below or Red Hill and Main Ridge behind the hill.
Go early in school holidays; the summit and Eagle can get busy.

places.name: Balnarring
places.factualLede: Balnarring is a hinterland village on the Mornington Peninsula's eastern wine country, 80 km from Melbourne, near the Coolart wetlands and the monthly Emu Plains Market.
places.intro: Balnarring is the village that locals still treat as their own  -  a cluster of shops, a Thursday morning farmers' market, a bookshop that has outlasted all reasonable expectations, and a road network that somehow always seems to lead back to a cellar door. It sits on the eastern edge of the Peninsula's wine country, closer to Western Port than Port Phillip, and that changes the character: the light is softer, the crowds are thinner, and the vineyards here tend to be smaller family operations rather than destination estates. Balnarring is where you go when you want a Peninsula weekend that feels like the way things used to work before the region became a brand. The beach is genuine and quiet, the coffee is unpretentious, and the drive in from Tedesca or Montalto takes fifteen minutes of roads you've mostly never seen.
places.signature: The village the rest of the Peninsula forgets, with the best bakehouse on the bay side.
notFor: people who need a polished resort scene
places.stayDuration: half a day to one night
tldr: Balnarring is the Peninsula's quietest genuine village — Thursday farmers' market, a bookshop, a clean beach on Western Port, and wine-country roads nobody else is driving.
Best for: visitors who want the eastern hinterland; anyone who's had enough of Red Hill crowds; families who want a calm Western Port beach.
Signature experience: Thursday market, then one of the small family-run cellar doors on the eastern ridge.
Half a day; pairs naturally with Merricks or the Red Hill plateau.

places.name: Bittern
places.factualLede: Bittern is a small residential village on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port coast, 75 km from Melbourne, with a station on the Stony Point train line and a coastal wetland reserve known for wading birds.
places.intro: Bittern is a small Western-Port village named for the marsh bird that still nests in the coastal wetlands at its edge, and it has a thoroughly ordinary main street that conceals one of the most birdable shorelines on the Peninsula. The Bittern Coastal Wetlands  -  saltmarsh, mudflats, mangroves  -  are one of the least-promoted nature reserves in the region and one of the best places in Victoria to watch wading birds at low tide. The village itself is residential, with a station on the Stony Point train line and a general store. Bittern matters mostly as a stopping point: a wetland walk in the morning, a coffee on the main street, then drive south to Hastings or onward to Crib Point. There is little reason to stay here, every reason to stop for an hour or two if birds and quiet shorelines interest you.
places.signature: A working Western Port village hiding one of Victoria's best wading-bird wetlands at its edge.
tldr: Bittern is a small Western Port village with one of the Peninsula's best wading-bird wetlands and a station on the Stony Point train line.
Best for: birders; train-accessible day trippers; people building a Western Port loop with Hastings and Crib Point.
Signature experience: a low-tide walk through the Coastal Wetlands with binoculars, then coffee on the main street.
An hour or two; not a place to base for a weekend.
Carless travellers can reach it directly by train from Melbourne via Frankston.

places.name: Boneo
places.factualLede: Boneo is a rural locality on the Mornington Peninsula's southern back-beach belt between Rye and Cape Schanck, 90 km from Melbourne, home to the Boneo Maze, the Peninsula Hot Springs / Alba thermal-springs district and the RACV Cape Schanck Resort.
places.intro: Boneo is the rural triangle between Rye, the back beaches and Cape Schanck, and for most of its history it was almost entirely a farming district. It still feels that way  -  long straight roads through paddocks, horse studs, the occasional cellar door  -  but on the southern edge of the district sit Peninsula Hot Springs and RACV Cape Schanck Resort, two of the Peninsula's busiest visitor anchors. That gives Boneo an unusual character: a working agricultural pocket that happens to sit on top of geothermal water and next to a golf-and-spa resort. The Boneo Maze and Wetland is the family-friendly headline, but the real draw is the position  -  fifteen minutes from a soak, ten minutes from a back-beach walk, and twenty minutes from a long lunch in Red Hill. Stay here if you want the hot-springs belt at your door without the resort vibe.
places.signature: The quiet rural triangle that holds Peninsula Hot Springs, the Boneo Maze and Cape Schanck on three sides.
notFor: anyone wanting cafés in walking distance
tldr: Boneo is rural country that happens to sit beside Peninsula Hot Springs, Alba Thermal Springs and RACV Cape Schanck — a quieter base than Rye for the same belt.
Best for: families wanting the Boneo Maze plus a soak; golfers basing at RACV; visitors who want hot-springs proximity without staying inside a resort.
Signature experience: an afternoon at the maze with kids, a sundown soak, breakfast on the deck the next morning.
Two nights to do it properly; pair the soak with one of the back beaches.
Boneo is a district, not a village — there is no shop strip.

places.name: Cape Schanck
places.factualLede: Cape Schanck is the southernmost cape of the Mornington Peninsula, 95 km from Melbourne, marked by an 1859 lighthouse and the Bass Strait basalt coastline.
places.intro: Cape Schanck is where the Peninsula finally runs out of land, dropping off the plateau into Bass Strait with a drama that still takes first-timers by surprise. The 1859 lighthouse stands on the last headland, the boardwalk threads down through tea-tree to a basalt beach that disappears at high tide, and on a clear afternoon the horizon carries nothing but open ocean all the way to Tasmania. This is the Peninsula's most cinematic short walk, and the cleanest case for why the southern end is worth the drive beyond the vineyards. Come for the lighthouse and the lookout, stay for the Bushrangers Bay walk west along the coast, and time your arrival for the last two hours of daylight.
places.signature: The boardwalk at the tip of the headland, where the Southern Ocean comes in.
tldr: Cape Schanck is the Peninsula's most cinematic short walk — an 1859 lighthouse, basalt sea stacks, and the open Southern Ocean to the south.
Best for: walkers; photographers; anyone doing the Two Bays Walking Track or wanting Bushrangers Bay without a crowd.
Signature experience: the boardwalk to the basalt beach below the lighthouse, then the coastal walk west to Bushrangers Bay.
Half a day; arrive in the last two hours of daylight for the best light on the lighthouse.

places.name: Capel Sound
places.factualLede: Capel Sound is a bayside town on the Mornington Peninsula's Port Phillip coast immediately west of Rosebud, 75 km from Melbourne, with a long bay beach, the Rosebud Foreshore camping ground and a developing café strip.
places.intro: Capel Sound is the western half of what was, until 2017, simply called Rosebud West, and the renaming did the place a quiet favour. It is now its own town in the postcodes if not yet in everyone's mental map: a long stretch of bayside foreshore camping ground, a small but lengthening main road of cafés and surf shops, and a residential grid that runs back from the beach in long flat blocks. The Rosebud-Capel Sound foreshore camp is one of the largest beachfront camping grounds in Australia, and for two months every summer it doubles the population of the entire stretch. Outside that window Capel Sound is calm, flat, and uncomplicated  -  a town that locals use when they want a bay-side walk that isn't busy. Stay here for foreshore camping or a cheaper inland rental; for restaurants, walk or drive five minutes into Rosebud.
places.signature: The Peninsula's biggest beachfront camp ground and the quieter half of the Rosebud bay strip.
notFor: anyone wanting a dense restaurant strip
people who hate caravan crowds in January
places.stayDuration: two nights minimum, a fortnight if camping
tldr: Capel Sound is the bayside town west of Rosebud — long foreshore, one of Australia's biggest beachfront camp grounds, a flat residential grid behind.
Best for: summer foreshore campers; families wanting a calm bay base outside school holidays; renters chasing lower rates than Rosebud proper.
Signature experience: a long foreshore walk between Capel Sound and Rye at sunset, summer-camp life behind the dunes.
A weekend in shoulder seasons; longer for foreshore camping.
Treat Rosebud and Capel Sound as one continuous strip for restaurants.

places.name: Crib Point
places.factualLede: Crib Point is a small residential village on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port coast between Hastings and Stony Point, 80 km from Melbourne, with a station on the Stony Point train line and Woolleys Beach on the foreshore.
places.intro: Crib Point sits halfway between Hastings and Stony Point on the Western Port shoreline, a small village built around a navy history that quietly defined it for most of the twentieth century  -  HMAS Cerberus is its southern neighbour and the largest naval base in the country. The village is residential, with a station on the Stony Point train line and a few low-key streets that lead down to Woolleys Beach, a small shaded swimming pocket that locals know about and almost no visitors do. The Western Port coast here is mangrove and mudflat country, and walking south along the foreshore toward Stony Point at low tide is one of the better long, flat coastal walks on the Peninsula. Come here for the walks and the train; stay in Hastings for the meal.
places.signature: The walking village between Hastings and the Stony Point ferry — quiet, mangrove-edged, train-accessible.
tldr: Crib Point is the small residential village between Hastings and Stony Point — Woolleys Beach, a train station and a long foreshore walk toward the ferry.
Best for: walkers; carless travellers; people building the Western Port loop properly.
Signature experience: low-tide walk south along the foreshore toward Stony Point, ferry on, train back.
Half a day; pair with Hastings or Stony Point for a full day.
There is little to eat in the village — provision in Hastings.

places.name: Dromana
places.factualLede: Dromana is a bayside town on the Mornington Peninsula's eastern Port Phillip shoreline, 75 km from Melbourne, at the foot of Arthurs Seat State Park.
places.intro: Dromana is the town at the foot of Arthurs Seat, and the practical hinge between the bay road and the hinterland behind it. Look one way and the long shallow beach runs uninterrupted toward Safety Beach; look the other and the land climbs fast into pinot country. Because of that geography, Dromana has always carried more than its weight  -  it is where many of the Peninsula's founding wineries planted their first vines in the 1970s, where Crittenden and the Dromana Estate groundstock still sit, and where the ferry from the ocean side of the ridge puts locals back on the bay in fifteen minutes. The town itself is unpretentious: a foreshore, a pier, a post-war main drag quietly modernising. Use it as a base for Red Hill without paying Red Hill prices, swim in the morning, drive up for lunch, and come back down in time for a sunset on the beach.
places.signature: The gateway town — more accessible than the hinterland, still genuinely Peninsula.
notFor: people chasing a polished village feel
tldr: Dromana is the practical hinge between the bay and the hinterland — base camp for Arthurs Seat, the gondola, and the wine country immediately behind it.
Best for: families using it as a base for Arthurs Seat Eagle; wine visitors who want bay access; anyone who wants Red Hill proximity without Red Hill prices.
Signature experience: Arthurs Seat Eagle gondola in the morning, then drive up to a Red Hill cellar door for lunch.
Full day or overnight; pairs naturally with Safety Beach and Red Hill.

places.name: Fingal
places.factualLede: Fingal is a coastal village on the Mornington Peninsula's ocean-coast edge, 90 km from Melbourne, home to Peninsula Hot Springs and adjacent to Moonah Links golf resort and Cape Schanck.
places.intro: Fingal sits quietly between Rye and Cape Schanck on the Peninsula's ocean-coast flank, and it is the kind of place that earns its reputation through what happens there rather than through what it calls itself. Peninsula Hot Springs has made it a pilgrimage destination for a particular kind of weekend — thermal pools, early morning mist off the coast, a round at Moonah Links, and nothing much else demanding your attention. The Cape Schanck lighthouse is fifteen minutes south. The back beaches are wild and within reach. Fingal rewards the visitor who wants comfort rather than activity.
places.signature: The Peninsula's thermal heart — where the weekend slows all the way down.
notFor: anyone who wants to walk to dinner
places.worstTime: peak summer weekends — hot springs are crowded and book out weeks ahead
tldr: Fingal is the Peninsula's wellness and golf destination — Peninsula Hot Springs is here, Moonah Links is here, and Cape Schanck is a short drive south.
Best for: thermal wellness weekends, golf stays, couples who want luxury without Sorrento's crowds.
Signature experience: a morning thermal soak at Peninsula Hot Springs, then a round at Moonah Links, then nothing.
Two nights minimum — Fingal is about slowing down, not covering ground.

places.name: Flinders
places.factualLede: Flinders is a coastal village on the Mornington Peninsula's southern Bass Strait edge, 105 km from Melbourne, with a working pier, marine sanctuary and a ranked golf course.
places.intro: Flinders sits on the wild southern edge of the Peninsula and carries itself with a kind of salt-air confidence. The village is compact but smart  -  a bakery, a handful of good shops, an old pub, and a coastline that feels a world away from the bay-facing polish further north. Base yourself here if you want your mornings to begin with wind off Bass Strait, your afternoons with a drive back inland for lunch, and your evenings under a harder, cleaner sky.
places.signature: The village that the Peninsula keeps to itself.
bestFor: people who already know the Peninsula
tldr: Flinders is the Peninsula's most complete ocean-coast village — a bakery, a pub, a world-class golf course, and a marine sanctuary immediately offshore.
Best for: serious golfers; divers after the Flinders Blowhole; anyone who wants a southern-edge village base without driving to the tip.
Signature experience: walk the coastal reserve past the blowhole at high tide, then a long lunch in the village.
Full day; Flinders rewards staying rather than passing through.

places.name: Hastings
places.factualLede: Hastings is a port town on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port shoreline, 75 km from Melbourne, with a Thursday street market and a working commercial harbour on the eastern bay.
places.intro: Hastings sits on the eastern, working side of the Peninsula  -  the Western Port side, with its mangroves, mudflats, and fishing fleet. It is not a tourist town and never has tried to be, which is exactly what makes it useful. The fishermen's co-op here supplies some of the best seafood in Melbourne, the mussel farms offshore are among the largest sustainable producers in Australia, and if you are driving back from French Island or heading down to Flinders the long way round, Hastings is the place to stop for fish and chips eaten on the pier. The town itself is unvarnished in a way the western Peninsula no longer is, and that counts for something.
places.signature: The Peninsula's working port, where the seafood is better than the streetscape.
places.bestSeason: winter for mussels and clear air
tldr: Hastings is the Peninsula's working port town — a fishermen's co-op, mussel farms offshore, and a Stony Point ferry to Phillip Island that most visitors don't know exists.
Best for: seafood lovers; anyone travelling to French Island or Phillip Island by ferry; travellers arriving by train from Melbourne.
Half a day; stop for fish and chips on the pier, then continue south.

places.name: Main Ridge
places.factualLede: Main Ridge is a hinterland village on the Mornington Peninsula's central wine plateau, 90 km from Melbourne, the highest part of the cool-climate pinot noir country.
places.intro: Main Ridge is the highest part of the Peninsula wine country, and the most forgiving to pinot noir. A few degrees cooler than Red Hill proper, wetter in winter, and foggy on the right mornings  -  if you drew the perfect place to grow cool-climate grapes in Victoria, it would look something like this. There is no real village centre, just a crossroads, a hall, and a handful of the most serious cellar doors on the Peninsula scattered through ferny side roads. Main Ridge rewards people who want to understand wine country rather than just photograph it: the single-vineyard bottles from this sub-region are consistently among the region's best, the estates are small and run by the people who own them, and nobody is trying to sell you a wedding venue. Come for a morning tasting at one of the serious producers, then drive ten minutes in any direction for lunch.
places.signature: The highest point on the Peninsula, where the pinot is best and the road narrows.
bestFor: the most focused cellar door day
notFor: anyone trying to cram five stops into one day
places.worstTime: rainy winter weekdays when venues shut early
tldr: Main Ridge is the most rural locality in the Mornington Peninsula hinterland — no cafés, no boutiques, just farmland, bush, and cellar doors.
Best for: wine tourists who want something unhurried; walkers with an eye for wildlife; anyone overdoing Sorrento and needing to recalibrate.
Signature experience: Greens Bush at dusk when the eastern grey kangaroos emerge.
Half-day is sufficient; pair with Red Hill for a full day.

places.name: McCrae
places.factualLede: McCrae is a small bayside town on the Mornington Peninsula's Port Phillip coast between Dromana and Rosebud, 75 km from Melbourne, anchored by McCrae Lighthouse, McCrae Homestead and a calm bayside swimming beach.
places.intro: McCrae sits quietly between Dromana and Rosebud, often skipped over by people who treat the bay drive as a single line  -  which is a shame, because it has the best small-town beach on this stretch and the oldest building still standing on the Peninsula. The McCrae Lighthouse is the postcard, and Andrew McCrae's 1844 homestead, still set in its original garden, is the kind of history that survives only by being mostly forgotten. The foreshore here is a clean, gently shelving bay beach with bathing boxes and a long swimming pier, and the residential streets behind run up to the foot of Arthurs Seat. It is the sort of town that locals on the Peninsula use as a base when Dromana is too busy and Rosebud is too sprawling. Stay here for calm-water swimming and the back-of-Arthurs lookout walks; do not come for nightlife.
places.signature: Bayside swimming, a lighthouse, and the Peninsula's oldest homestead — the bay's quiet middle.
notFor: anyone chasing a busy restaurant strip
tldr: McCrae is the in-between bay town most visitors skip — calm beach, the Peninsula's oldest homestead, a lighthouse, and the back of Arthurs Seat right behind.
Best for: families wanting calmer bay swimming than Dromana; history-minded travellers; walkers using the Arthurs Seat trails.
Signature experience: morning swim from the bathing boxes, a wander through McCrae Homestead garden, lighthouse photo at dusk.
A weekend works well; pair with Dromana or Rosebud for dining.
Quieter at the foreshore than its neighbours, especially out of school holidays.

places.name: Merricks
places.factualLede: Merricks is a hinterland village on the Mornington Peninsula's southern wine country, 90 km from Melbourne, anchored by the Merricks General Wine Store crossroads.
places.intro: Merricks is where the Peninsula's wine country starts to feel private. There is almost no main street to speak of, just a low-slung hall, winding vineyard roads, and a cluster of estates and restaurants that reward people who know where to turn off. The light is softer here than in Red Hill proper and the bay feels unexpectedly close. It is one of the Peninsula's best places to stay if your idea of a weekend away means vines outside the window, lunch that goes too long, and very little noise.
places.signature: A quiet corridor between the ridge and the bay, with the best wine shop on the Peninsula.
bestFor: the stop that holds a day together
notFor: people who need lots of shops
tldr: Merricks is a small rural village that punches above its size — Pt Leo Estate alone makes it worth the detour.
Best for: serious wine and art visitors; walkers on the Red Hill Rail Trail; people who value understatement.
Signature experience: lunch at Pt Leo Estate with the sculpture park, then a walk to Merricks Beach.
Half a day to a full day. No accommodation within the village itself.

places.name: Merricks Beach
places.factualLede: Merricks Beach is a small residential hamlet on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port coast, 80 km from Melbourne, with a shallow tide-dependent beach and no commercial centre.
places.intro: Merricks Beach is a hamlet, not a town, and is largely the work of one generation of holiday-house builders who put up timber shacks along the dunes in the 1950s and 60s and then refused to let the place change much since. The beach is shallow, tide-dependent, and quiet  -  there is no surf, no foreshore café strip, and at low tide it spreads out into hundreds of metres of flat sand that visiting children turn into a private kingdom. The Merricks General Store, technically up in Merricks village, is the one polished thing nearby and is famous for a reason. Stay at Merricks Beach if you want the holiday-house feeling the Peninsula has mostly lost: front-door dunes, no shops, neighbours you have to walk past, and an evening rhythm built around a sundowner on the verandah.
places.signature: A 1950s holiday-house hamlet with a tide-flat beach and no commercial centre — the Peninsula's quietest piece of coast.
tldr: Merricks Beach is a 1950s-built holiday-house hamlet on a shallow Western Port beach — quiet, low-rise, no shops.
Best for: families with small children; couples wanting a slow weekend; anyone who values the old holiday-house Peninsula feeling.
Signature experience: low-tide afternoon on the sand flats, sundowner on the verandah, dinner from Merricks General Store the next day.
Two nights minimum; mid-week off-season is the best version.
There is no shop — pre-buy in Balnarring or Merricks village.

places.name: Merricks North
places.factualLede: Merricks North is a small wine-country locality on the Mornington Peninsula's red-hill plateau, 80 km from Melbourne, home to Elgee Park, Baillieu, Stonier and other established cool-climate cellar doors.
places.intro: Merricks North is wine country with a quieter accent than Red Hill and a longer pedigree than the Merricks village down the road. The roads here run between vineyards that were planted in the 1970s and 1980s  -  Elgee Park, Baillieu, Stonier  -  back when the Peninsula's cool-climate Pinot was an experiment most people did not believe in. The result is a small dense pocket of cellar doors with serious wines and almost no signage, hedged in by polo fields, horse studs, and one of the prettier country halls on the Peninsula. There is no town centre, no general store, and that is part of the point. Drive in for a slow cellar-door morning, lunch held at a vineyard restaurant, and an afternoon detour to the Merricks beach side if the weather allows. Stay nearby in Merricks or Red Hill; come here to drink.
places.signature: The older, quieter half of the Peninsula's wine country — pioneer vineyards on quiet country lanes.
bestFor: couples on a long lunch weekend
places.stayDuration: a long lunch, or a night in Merricks
tldr: Merricks North is the older, quieter wine pocket above Merricks village — Elgee Park, Baillieu, Stonier and a polo field on a country road.
Best for: serious wine visitors; people who already know Red Hill and want something quieter.
Signature experience: three cellar doors and a long lunch over a Sunday, finished with a drive down to Point Leo for sunset.
Half a day for the wines; an overnight in Merricks or Red Hill rounds it out.
There is no village centre — choose your day around the cellar doors, not a main street.

places.name: Moorooduc
places.factualLede: Moorooduc is a rural hinterland locality on the Mornington Peninsula's northern edge, 65 km from Melbourne, known for the Moorooduc Estate vineyard and the Mornington Peninsula Steam Railway.
places.intro: Moorooduc is the wine country's quieter northern edge — further from the ridge road, less visited, different enough in soil and latitude to grow serious chardonnay that the broader market still underrates. Moorooduc Estate and Barmah Park are the anchors. Use it for a slow cellar-door morning before heading up to Red Hill for lunch.
places.signature: The overlooked northern wine pocket where serious producers work without the Red Hill fuss.
tldr: Moorooduc is a small hinterland locality that most visitors pass through on Moorooduc Highway rather than stop in — the ones who do stop find it quiet and unhurried.
Best for: families with small children interested in the heritage railway; walkers looking for an accessible quarry walk; anyone exploring the northern hinterland.
Half a day is sufficient.

places.name: Mornington
places.factualLede: Mornington is the gateway town to the Mornington Peninsula on the Port Phillip Bay shore, 60 km from Melbourne, with a Wednesday foreshore farmers' market and the Esplanade bathing-box stretch.
places.intro: Mornington was the gateway town for a long time — the first real stop on the road south, somewhere to buy petrol before pressing on to beaches and vineyards. That undersells it now. A genuinely good main street, a Wednesday farmers' market on the Esplanade worth getting up for, a foreshore with bathing boxes and a saltwater pool — Mornington has quietly become a whole-day destination rather than a waypoint. It's also the most practical Peninsula base: north to Mount Martha's beaches, south to Red Hill's vineyards, fifteen minutes from coast in either direction.
places.signature: The commercial hub — the most town-like part of the Peninsula, still worth knowing.
notFor: travellers who only care about wineries
places.worstTime: Main Street on hot summer Saturdays
tldr: Mornington is the Peninsula's most complete town — a real main street, a Wednesday farmers' market, bathing boxes, and serious restaurants all within reach of each other.
Best for: couples and families wanting a full-day town experience; anyone who wants a practical base with easy access north and south.
Signature experience: Wednesday Esplanade market followed by a walk along the foreshore to Schnapper Point.
Half a day easily; a full day with the market and a long lunch.

places.name: Mount Eliza
places.factualLede: Mount Eliza is an affluent bayside town on the Mornington Peninsula's northern Port Phillip coast, 50 km from Melbourne, anchored by a village café strip and a string of small bay beaches including Canadian Bay and Ranelagh.
places.intro: Mount Eliza is the Peninsula's northern threshold and, depending on how you read it, either its most affluent commuter suburb or its most underrated bay-side town. Both are true. The village strip on Mount Eliza Way is short, well-fed and self-aware  -  a few of the best independent cafés on the Peninsula are here  -  and the back streets fall down to a string of small bay beaches that locals have managed to keep more or less to themselves. Canadian Bay is the headline; Ranelagh has the postcard staircase; Sunnyside is the unofficial nudist beach for the brave. The town is independent-school country  -  Toorak, Peninsula Grammar, St Catherine's  -  which sets a particular weekend cadence: tennis-club mornings, café brunches, school-pickup-hour traffic. Stay here if you want a base that is closer to Melbourne than the rest of the Peninsula and quietly better-fed than its neighbours.
places.signature: The Peninsula's underrated northern village — quietly the best brunch strip and the closest bay beaches to Melbourne.
notFor: anyone chasing wineries on their doorstep
people who measure the Peninsula by Sorrento
places.stayDuration: a long day, or a first night
tldr: Mount Eliza is the Peninsula's affluent northern gateway — a tight village strip with strong cafés, and a string of small bay beaches the rest of Melbourne has mostly missed.
Best for: brunch-driven day-trippers; families using Canadian Bay; anyone wanting Peninsula proximity without driving to Sorrento.
Signature experience: early walk to Canadian Bay, breakfast on the village strip, afternoon swim at Ranelagh.
A great day trip; an easy first night for a longer Peninsula weekend.
Closest Peninsula town to Melbourne — practical for a no-pack mid-week visit.

places.name: Mount Martha
places.factualLede: Mount Martha is a bayside town on the Mornington Peninsula's eastern Port Phillip shore, 70 km from Melbourne, between Mornington and Dromana, with the most photographed bathing boxes on the bay.
places.intro: Mount Martha is the Peninsula's best-kept secret for people who only want to do one thing: stop. This is swimming-beach country  -  a long, gentle curve of pale sand with bathing boxes at the northern end, south-facing enough to catch afternoon sun, and sheltered enough from the wind to be usable almost nine months of the year. The village proper sits up on the hill, compact and quiet, with a bakery, a few cafes, and enough infrastructure to get through a weekend without ever needing to drive further than the beach. South of the village, the coastal track winds toward the Briars wetlands and eventually down to Mornington; north, it runs into the foreshore reserve and the bathing boxes. It is the simplest, cleanest Peninsula day on Port Phillip: swim, walk, coffee, repeat.
places.signature: The most liveable part of the Peninsula — where the beach meets the suburb properly.
notFor: people who want the busiest Peninsula action
tldr: Mount Martha is the Peninsula's most scenic bay-coast village — a long pale arc of beach backed by low hills, quieter than anything south of Mornington.
Best for: families who want a clean, uncrowded bay beach; walkers on the coastal track to the Briars; anyone who wants to stop and stay stopped.
Signature experience: morning swim at the bathing boxes end, then the coastal track south toward the Briars wetlands.
Half a day is enough; a full day if you add the Briars walk.

places.name: Point Leo
places.factualLede: Point Leo is a small coastal locality on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port coast, 85 km from Melbourne, anchored by a long-standing surf break, the Point Leo Foreshore Reserve camp ground and Point Leo Estate's sculpture park, restaurant and cellar door.
places.intro: Point Leo is a beach, a surf break, and one of the most ambitious privately held sculpture parks in the country  -  and almost nothing else. The village barely qualifies as a village  -  a foreshore camping ground, a surf life-saving club, a quiet residential pocket  -  but pull off the road into Point Leo Estate and you find sixteen hectares of contemporary sculpture rolling toward the bay, a hatted dining room with one of the great Australian wine lists, and a cellar door that takes itself only as seriously as it should. The break out front is the Peninsula's most consistent right-hander, and the longboard contest that turns up here each year is the real local calendar. People come to Point Leo for a quiet morning at the beach, an unhurried afternoon among the sculptures, and a long dinner with a Pinot Noir flight. That sequence is the entire reason to come.
places.signature: Sixteen hectares of contemporary sculpture rolling toward Western Port — and one of the Peninsula's quietest surf breaks out front.
notFor: people wanting a village to walk
first-time Peninsula visitors with one day
places.stayDuration: a full day, or a night on the foreshore
tldr: Point Leo is two things — one of the Peninsula's most consistent surf breaks, and Point Leo Estate's hatted restaurant, cellar door and 16-hectare sculpture park.
Best for: art lovers; surfers; serious food-and-wine visitors who want a single-stop day.
Signature experience: morning walk through the sculptures, lunch on the Estate verandah, afternoon at the break.
A full day even if you skip dinner; pair it with Shoreham or Flinders for a weekend.
The foreshore camping ground is among the Peninsula's best for beach-front sites.

places.name: Point Nepean
places.factualLede: Point Nepean is the western tip of the Mornington Peninsula, 100 km from Melbourne, a national park covering the historic quarantine station, fortifications and the entry to Port Phillip Bay.
places.intro: Point Nepean is the Peninsula at its most exposed and historically strange: quarantine station buildings facing the bay, old gun emplacements buried in coastal scrub, and walking tracks that keep revealing a new view across Port Phillip Heads just when you think the drama has peaked. It is less a single attraction than a whole day of edges  -  military ruins, tea-tree, pale water, and the sense that Melbourne has fallen clean away behind you. Go early, wear proper shoes, and give yourself time to keep stopping at the lookouts.
places.signature: The end of the Peninsula, where military ruins and ocean light do the same job of making Melbourne feel very far away.
notFor: anyone wanting a casual quick stop
tldr: Point Nepean National Park is the Peninsula's most dramatic walk — quarantine station ruins, gun emplacements, and views across Port Phillip Heads at the continent's edge.
Best for: walkers; history enthusiasts; anyone who wants to understand the Peninsula beyond its wine and beach reputation.
Signature experience: the Forts Walk from the visitor centre to Fort Nepean, timed to arrive at the headland in the last two hours of light.
Entry is free; a shuttle runs along the old army road to the fort precinct.
Full day; go early and stay late.

places.name: Portsea
places.factualLede: Portsea is a coastal village at the western tip of the Mornington Peninsula, 100 km from Melbourne, with a heritage front beach, a back beach on Bass Strait and the gateway to Point Nepean National Park.
places.intro: Portsea is the Peninsula's quiet trophy. Where Sorrento turns on the theatre, Portsea keeps its back to the bay and its gates closed  -  this is old-money country, where the holiday houses were built before anyone called them beach houses and the golf club is older than most Australian cities. The village itself is barely a village: a pub, a general store, a scattering of shops around the foreshore, and a short walk down to a jetty that still looks essentially as it did a century ago. But push past the surface and Portsea is the entry point for the whole south-western tip of the Peninsula: Point Nepean is next door, the back-beach surf is five minutes away, and the front beach is one of the most protected swims on Port Phillip. Come for a long lunch at the pub, a quiet morning walk before the day-trippers find Sorrento, or a summer weekend that stays deliberately low-key.
places.signature: The most private end of the Peninsula — the back beach is one of the best in Victoria.
tldr: Portsea is the Peninsula's final town and most quietly exclusive — old holiday houses behind gates, a pub on the foreshore, and Point Nepean National Park next door.
Best for: visitors who want Point Nepean; surfers heading to the back beach; anyone curious what old Peninsula money looks like.
Signature experience: long lunch at the pub, then walk or cycle into Point Nepean for the afternoon.
Half a day; usually paired with Point Nepean and Sorrento.

places.name: Red Hill
places.factualLede: Red Hill is the central hinterland village of the Mornington Peninsula's wine country, 85 km from Melbourne, on a cool-climate basalt plateau between Western Port and Port Phillip.
places.intro: On a misty basalt plateau above the Peninsula's central ridge, Red Hill has arranged some of the strongest food and wine in Victoria into a circuit that rewards the unhurried. A village by strict measure — a general store, a monthly market, vineyard restaurants that don't advertise from the highway — it nonetheless organises the whole upper Peninsula around itself. The winery restaurant cluster here — Ten Minutes by Tractor, Montalto, Paringa Estate, Principia — has no serious peer in the state. Come on Saturday; plan lunch first.
places.signature: The most concentrated food and wine precinct on the Peninsula, on the plateau above the bay.
notFor: people trying to do the Peninsula cheaply
tldr: Red Hill is the Mornington Peninsula's wine and food epicentre — specifically Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and orchards producing apples and cherries.
Best for: wine tourists, serious eaters, weekend stays that centre on food rather than beach.
Signature experience: cellar door Saturday followed by the Red Hill Market, then lunch at a vineyard restaurant.
Spend at least one full day; two nights if you're here for wine.
No beach within five minutes — that's not what Red Hill is for.

places.name: Red Hill South
places.factualLede: Red Hill South is a quiet rural locality on the lower Red Hill plateau on the Mornington Peninsula, 85 km from Melbourne, with a country pub, established cellar doors and a high concentration of farmhouse bed-and-breakfasts.
places.intro: Red Hill South is the lower, quieter half of the Red Hill plateau, and for visitors who already know the headline village it is often the better stay. The roads drop down off the ridge into a softer landscape  -  a community shop, a small handful of cellar doors, a popular country pub, and a long catalogue of bed-and-breakfasts in renovated farmhouses. The cellar doors here  -  Foxeys Hangout, Quealy, Lindenderry  -  pull a different crowd to the ridge-top names, and the lunch options below Red Hill village proper are some of the most rewarding on the Peninsula. The Red Hill Market on the first Saturday of the month sits between the two villages and is genuinely the best market on the Peninsula. Stay here when the upper village is full or when you want a cellar-door weekend that is slightly off the obvious circuit.
places.signature: The quieter, lower-elevation half of the Peninsula's wine country — better B&Bs, fewer crowds, the same cellar-door belt.
notFor: first-time visitors who haven't seen Red Hill village
tldr: Red Hill South is the lower-elevation half of the Red Hill plateau — same wine country, quieter roads, more bed-and-breakfasts than its better-known neighbour.
Best for: returning Peninsula visitors who already know Red Hill; couples on a B&B weekend; market shoppers.
Signature experience: Red Hill Market on a first Saturday morning, then a long lunch at one of the lower cellar doors.
A weekend; two nights minimum to see the cellar doors properly.
Less foot traffic than Red Hill village proper — book the cellar doors but you will not be queuing.

places.name: Rosebud
places.factualLede: Rosebud is a bayside town on the Mornington Peninsula's southern Port Phillip shoreline, 85 km from Melbourne, with an 8 km foreshore camping reserve and a long shallow swimming beach.
places.intro: Rosebud is the largest of the bayside towns and the one locals use when they actually want something done  -  a supermarket, a hardware store, an everyday main street that has not yet been aestheticised into a postcard. That practicality is also its charm. The beach is long and genuinely good, with a sheltered swimming area and grass right up to the sand; the jetty is a quiet fishing spot at dusk; and a string of ethnic kitchens along Point Nepean Road provide the kind of honest, unheralded lunches that make a weekend on the Peninsula feel less like a brochure and more like a real place. Use Rosebud as your resupply stop, but don't rush through it.
places.signature: The practical bay town where the beach is better than the reputation suggests.
notFor: visitors who want to stay only at the fashionable end of the Peninsula
tldr: Rosebud is the Peninsula's most liveable bay town — long foreshore, practical main street, and a beach that genuinely delivers without requiring effort.
Best for: families who need a full-service town; foreshore campers; day visitors who want a long beach walk and an honest lunch.
Signature experience: morning swim, pier walk at dusk, dinner at one of the unpretentious ethnic kitchens on Point Nepean Road.
Half a day to full day; foreshore camping makes it a natural overnight stop.

places.name: Rye
places.factualLede: Rye is a coastal town on the Mornington Peninsula's southern Port Phillip shore, 90 km from Melbourne, with a back beach on Bass Strait, the Rye Pier, and a foreshore that fills with summer holidaymakers.
places.intro: Rye is the pivot point of the lower Peninsula  -  the last town before Sorrento and Portsea, the first one where the landscape really opens up to the Southern Ocean. The front beach is a long bay-calm stretch with a pier and a century of summer memory behind it; the back beach is where you drive to in ten minutes to remind yourself that the ocean side is an entirely different country. In between sits a main street that has quietly improved itself over the past five years, a brewery precinct in the hills above the town, and Peninsula Hot Springs close enough to slot into an afternoon without rearranging the day. Rye is where families have always come to do nothing in particular, and that remains the right instinct.
places.signature: The Peninsula town that gives you the calm bay, the surf beach and the hot springs without making you choose.
bestFor: families who want bay and ocean access
notFor: people wanting a refined village feel
tldr: Rye is the Peninsula's two-beach town — calm bay front, wild ocean back, with Peninsula Hot Springs and a brewery in between.
Best for: families who want both bay and ocean in one base; divers; visitors who want Peninsula Hot Springs without driving further south.
Signature experience: morning swim on the front beach, afternoon at Peninsula Hot Springs, back beach walk at dusk.
Full day or overnight; the most practical base for the lower Peninsula outside Sorrento.

places.name: Safety Beach
places.factualLede: Safety Beach is a bayside township on the Mornington Peninsula's eastern Port Phillip shoreline, 70 km from Melbourne, between Dromana and Mount Martha, with a marina and a sheltered swimming beach.
places.intro: Safety Beach is the long shallow crescent between Mount Martha and Dromana  -  the kind of bay beach where the water is calm enough for very small children and the ridge behind it is steep enough to put you among vineyards in under ten minutes. For most of its history it was a quiet caravan-and-holiday-house stretch; in the last decade it has slowly sharpened, with a marina at the western end, a handful of smarter houses lining the foreshore, and a couple of genuinely good food stops using the view properly. It is a useful place to stay for anyone who wants a base that works equally for beach mornings and hinterland afternoons.
places.signature: The calmest broad bay foreshore on the Peninsula, with the ridge rising straight behind it.
notFor: anyone wanting a distinct town centre
places.worstTime: windless holiday afternoons when the foreshore is packed
places.stayDuration: half a day to one night
tldr: Safety Beach is a long, calm bay foreshore between Mount Martha and Dromana — shallow water makes it the Peninsula's best swimming spot for young children.
Best for: families with toddlers; anyone who wants calm water and easy beach access without driving to the crowded spots.
Signature experience: morning on the foreshore, then ten minutes up the hill to a cellar door or the Arthurs Seat gondola.
Half a day; usually paired with Dromana.

places.name: Shoreham
places.factualLede: Shoreham is a small coastal village on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port shoreline, 95 km from Melbourne, with a foreshore reserve, a beach swimming pool at low tide, and Pier 10 vineyard nearby.
places.intro: Shoreham barely qualifies as a village, and that is exactly its charm. A store, a hall, a tangle of narrow roads threading down to one of the loveliest small beaches on the Peninsula, and a handful of vineyards and olive groves that quietly produce some of the region's best fruit. The beach is family-scaled and protected enough for children, the bush behind it runs into Point Leo, and the drive up onto the ridge puts you in cellar door country within ten minutes. This is where locals go when the southern beaches start to feel loud and the long weekend crowd has swallowed Sorrento. Park once, walk to the beach, and stay until the light goes.
places.signature: A tiny coastal settlement where bush, vineyard and beach sit almost on top of each other.
notFor: anyone wanting lots of dining options
tldr: Shoreham is the most quietly beautiful small beach on the Western Port coast — a family-scaled foreshore backed by bush, with cellar doors ten minutes up the ridge.
Best for: artists; walkers linking to Point Leo or the Two Bays trail; anyone who needs to recalibrate after a day on the Sorrento side.
Signature experience: Honeysuckle Beach at low tide, then drive up to one of the ridge cellar doors for a quiet afternoon.
Half a day; best as a deliberate detour rather than a destination.

places.name: Somers
places.factualLede: Somers is a quiet residential village on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port coast, 80 km from Melbourne, fronting a long sheltered beach and bordering Coolart Wetlands and Homestead Reserve.
places.intro: Somers is the quiet Western Port answer to the bay-side beach villages, and it has been keeping that profile low on purpose for a century. The village is set back from a long shallow beach with tea-tree banking the dunes, a small general store, a yacht club that has changed almost nothing about itself since the 1950s, and not much else. Coolart Wetlands and Homestead, set in its 87-hectare reserve on the village edge, is the other reason to come  -  one of the best places to walk a wetland boardwalk under a winter sky on the entire Peninsula. The Lord Somers Camp gives the village a residual association with leadership weeks and a particular kind of Australian institutional history. Stay here if you want a beach village without polish, where the loudest sound in the morning is birds in the reserve.
places.signature: A sheltered Western Port beach and a wetland reserve at the village edge — the quiet Peninsula at full strength.
tldr: Somers is a deliberately quiet Western Port beach village — long sheltered beach, tea-tree dunes, a 1950s-era yacht club, and the Coolart wetlands on the edge.
Best for: birders; families wanting flat, safe wading water; readers who want to disappear into a holiday-house weekend.
Signature experience: a dawn walk through Coolart wetlands, then a long swim from the beach when the tide is in.
Two nights minimum, ideally midweek in spring.
There is no restaurant strip — pre-book in Balnarring or self-cater.

places.name: Sorrento
places.factualLede: Sorrento is a coastal town near the western tip of the Mornington Peninsula, 100 km from Melbourne, with a limestone-cliff main street, a ferry to Queenscliff and back-beach ocean baths carved into the rock.
places.intro: Sorrento is where the Peninsula narrows to a point and the social temperature rises. This is old-money beach culture done with increasing sophistication  -  limestone cliffs, a ferry to Queenscliff across the Heads, ocean baths carved from rock at low tide  -  alongside a main street that has quietly evolved into something genuinely worth driving for. The summer crowd is real and relentless, but the town earns it. Off-season Sorrento is a revelation: the light changes, the restaurants empty out to their best selves, and you can walk the ocean beach from one end to the other without encountering anyone but locals. The back beach at dusk is one of the best things on the Peninsula, full stop. Stay at least two nights.
places.signature: Ocean baths carved from limestone at the tip of the Peninsula.
tldr: Sorrento is the Peninsula's most celebrated town — limestone cliffs, ocean baths carved from rock, a ferry to Queenscliff across the Heads, and a main street that has earned its reputation.
Best for: first-time Peninsula visitors; romantic weekends; food and wine visitors who want a tip-of-the-Peninsula base.
Signature experience: ocean baths at dawn, then walk the back beach to the limestone cliffs before the day-trippers arrive.
Two nights minimum to see it properly; off-season is a revelation.
Summer crowds are real — book ahead or come in autumn.

places.name: St Andrews Beach
places.factualLede: St Andrews Beach is a coastal village on the Mornington Peninsula's back-beach coast between Rye and Cape Schanck, 90 km from Melbourne, anchored by a long ocean beach, the St Andrews Beach Brewery and the Boneo Park equestrian venue nearby.
places.intro: St Andrews Beach is what the Peninsula's back beaches look like when no one is trying. It sits between Rye and Cape Schanck, low and unstructured  -  a grid of holiday houses scattered through tea-tree and a long, raw ocean beach that locals still treat as their own. The pub here is a brewery, the brewery is a destination, and the destination doesn't care if you turn up in board shorts and sand. Surfers know the breaks; equestrians know the dressage venue; everyone else mostly just knows the brewery. The village has no centre to speak of, which is most of its charm  -  this is a place you base yourself for the dunes, the surf, and the long pour at sunset, not for boutiques or brunch culture. Off-season it empties out almost entirely. Stay then if you can.
places.signature: Back-beach surf country with the Peninsula's best brewery for a sunset.
notFor: anyone wanting cafés in walking distance
tldr: St Andrews Beach is a back-beach village built around surf, dunes and the St Andrews Beach Brewery — minimal village, maximum coast.
Best for: surfers; brewery long-lunchers; equestrians; anyone who wants Cape Schanck on their doorstep without driving to it.
Signature experience: a morning walk down the beach toward Gunnamatta, lunch at the Brewery, sunset back at the dunes.
Two nights minimum to feel it; off-season the village belongs to locals and dogs.
There is no main street and no supermarket — provision before you arrive.

places.name: Stony Point
places.factualLede: Stony Point is the southern terminus of the Stony Point railway line on the Mornington Peninsula's Western Port coast, 85 km from Melbourne, with a working fishing jetty and a passenger ferry to French Island and Phillip Island.
places.intro: Stony Point is the smallest possible village  -  a jetty, a ferry terminal, a railway terminus, a fishermen's hut or two  -  and one of the most useful addresses on the Peninsula. The ferry from the jetty runs across Western Port to French Island and on to Cowes on Phillip Island, which makes Stony Point one of the few places on mainland Victoria you can step off a train and onto a boat. There is no town to wander  -  the village is barely a village  -  but the working pier is a real fishing community and the views across to French Island catch the afternoon light beautifully. Park here, walk the jetty, take the ferry, or just sit on the pier with fish and chips brought down from Hastings. Stony Point is a transit point that rewards being treated as a destination for a few hours.
places.signature: The only point in Victoria where you step off a train and onto a ferry across Western Port.
notFor: anyone expecting a village to wander
places.stayDuration: half a day for the ferry loop
tldr: Stony Point is a jetty, a ferry terminal and a train terminus — the rare Australian point where you step off a train and onto a boat.
Best for: French Island day trippers; Phillip Island connectors; carless travellers who want to leave the car at Frankston.
Signature experience: train to Stony Point, ferry to French Island for a cycle, ferry back, fish and chips on the jetty.
Half a day for the ferry loop; a full day including French Island.
There is nothing to eat at the terminal — bring it from Hastings.

places.name: Tootgarook
places.factualLede: Tootgarook is a small village on the Mornington Peninsula's southern Port Phillip coast between Rye and Capel Sound, 80 km from Melbourne, with a calm bay beach across the highway and the Tootgarook Wetland reserve behind the dunes.
places.intro: Tootgarook is a small, mostly residential village squeezed between Rye and Capel Sound, and its real identity lives behind the streets in the Tootgarook Wetland  -  the largest privately-protected freshwater wetland on the Peninsula and a quiet ecological headline most visitors do not know exists. Out front, the village sits across the road from a wide bay beach with shallow water and a long pier; out back, the wetland soaks into the dunes and the migratory bird counts each spring are among the highest on the Peninsula. The village itself has a handful of shops and an unfussy main street and is almost entirely a place locals use. Stay nearby for cheaper Peninsula accommodation than Rye or Sorrento; come to walk the wetland boardwalk and read birds in the reeds.
places.signature: A modest bayside village hiding the Peninsula's largest freshwater wetland behind its dunes.
notFor: anyone wanting a dining scene at the doorstep
first-time Peninsula visitors with one day
tldr: Tootgarook is a quiet bayside village with the Peninsula's largest freshwater wetland reserve behind the dunes.
Best for: birders; budget weekenders looking for a Rye-adjacent base; families using the bay beach.
Signature experience: a spring morning walking the Tootgarook Wetland boardwalk, then a swim from the bayside pier.
A weekend; pair with Rye, Boneo and the back beaches for a full Peninsula loop.
There is little to eat in the village — walk into Rye for restaurants.

places.name: Tuerong
places.factualLede: Tuerong is a rural hinterland locality on the Mornington Peninsula's northern wine country, 70 km from Melbourne, known for the Quealy Winemakers cellar door and the Devilbend Reservoir.
places.intro: Tuerong is where some of the Peninsula's best bottles come from roads most visitors never take. Yabby Lake is the anchor — Halliday Top 100, relaxed cellar-door program — and the same back roads hold Dexter Wines and a cluster of low-volume producers whose fruit ends up in Melbourne's better wine lists. Quiet, specific, worth the detour.
places.signature: The wine-country back door, where some of the Peninsula's best bottles come from roads most visitors never take.
notFor: people wanting a village to walk around
tldr: Tuerong is a rural locality best known to wine enthusiasts as the address of Yabby Lake Vineyard and Dromana Estate.
Best for: serious wine visitors; walkers at Devilbend Reservoir; travellers who want hinterland quiet without driving all the way to Red Hill.
Half a day; usually paired with Moorooduc or Mornington.

places.name: Tyabb
places.factualLede: Tyabb is a small town on the Mornington Peninsula's northern Western Port flank, 65 km from Melbourne, anchored by the Tyabb Packing House antiques district and the Tyabb Air Show held at the grass airfield each autumn.
places.intro: Tyabb is the Peninsula's antique town and, twice a year, its airshow town, and for the rest of the calendar it is a small Western-Port-adjacent farming village most visitors drive past on the way to somewhere else. The antiques district is unusual  -  a long shed-filled lane known as Tyabb Packing House, half barn, half market, full of dealers who have been there for thirty years and know exactly what they have. The Old Tyabb airfield, a working grass strip on the edge of town, hosts the Tyabb Air Show each March and is home to one of Australia's best-known warbird collections. Beyond those two anchors, Tyabb is residential and rural  -  horse paddocks, a small main street, a bakery worth pulling over for. Come for an antique-hunting day with the airshow if the timing aligns; otherwise pair Tyabb with Hastings as a Western Port-side day.
places.signature: The Peninsula's antiques district and grass-strip airshow town — two reasons to take the back road.
notFor: first-time Peninsula visitors with one day
tldr: Tyabb has two anchors most visitors don't know about — Tyabb Packing House, the Peninsula's antique district, and the Tyabb Air Show on the grass airfield.
Best for: antique hunters; aviation enthusiasts; anyone building a Western-Port-side day with Hastings.
Signature experience: a half-day at Packing House, lunch at the bakery, then the air-show grass strip if the date aligns.
Half a day; pair with Hastings or Crib Point for the full Western-Port loop.
Train-accessible on the Stony Point line — a rare carless option for an antiques day.
